subject: 분배 정의와 운의 문제
title: Justice and the role of luck
content: Almost everyone agrees that people should not be worse off through no fault of their own, and yet the distribution of talents, families, and health is settled entirely by luck. Political philosophy has therefore asked how far justice requires us to correct for what nobody chose, and the answers proposed diverge sharply because the question touches both equality and responsibility at once. One influential position distinguishes what a person chose from what merely befell her. On this view inequalities that trace to genuine choices are acceptable, while those that trace to circumstance call for correction, and the boundary between them marks the limit of legitimate difference. The proposal seems to honour both values simultaneously, which is why it attracted so much attention. Its difficulties emerge when the boundary is examined. Whether a choice was genuine depends on the options available and on a character that was itself unchosen, so the distinction threatens to collapse once it is pressed. Critics add that the view treats those who chose badly with a harshness that most defenders of equality would reject, since it holds that they have no claim on assistance. A different tradition abandons the boundary and asks instead what arrangements free people could justify to one another. Luck then matters not because it is undeserved but because a scheme that ignored it could not be defended to those it disadvantaged.

subject: 동의는 무엇을 정당화하는가
title: What consent can justify
content: Consent transforms the moral character of an action, since what would otherwise be an assault becomes surgery and what would be theft becomes a gift. Moral philosophy therefore asks what gives agreement this power, and the question is pressing because consent is doing heavy work in medicine, law, and commerce, often in circumstances where its conditions are barely met. The standard account holds that consent expresses a person's authority over her own affairs, so agreement changes the moral situation because she is the one entitled to decide. This explains why consent obtained by deception fails, since the person agreed to something other than what occurred, and why consent under threat fails, since the choice was not hers in any meaningful sense. Both conditions are widely accepted and neither is easy to apply. Difficulties arise where the pressure is structural rather than personal. A worker who accepts dangerous conditions because the alternative is destitution has not been threatened by her employer, and yet calling her agreement free strains the concept. Some philosophers respond that consent remains valid while the background arrangement is unjust, separating two questions that are easily confused. Others hold that consent given under such constraint cannot justify what it purports to justify, and that treating it as valid launders the injustice that produced it.

subject: 설명과 인과의 관계
title: Explanation and its relation to causes
content: To explain why something happened is usually to say what brought it about, and this connection between explanation and causation seems so natural that it is often assumed without argument. Philosophers of science have nevertheless found reasons to separate the two, because several things we readily accept as explanations do not cite causes at all, and several causal statements explain nothing we wanted to know. Mathematical explanations illustrate the first case. Why a certain arrangement of objects cannot be divided evenly is answered by a fact about numbers rather than by anything that acted, and yet the answer plainly explains. Structural explanations work similarly, since saying that a population evolved a trait because of a constraint on possible forms does not name a cause acting on any individual. The second case is more common than it seems, because listing a cause of an event often leaves the question untouched. Knowing that a bridge fell because gravity pulled on it explains nothing, since gravity was pulling all along. What we wanted was the difference between this occasion and the others, which suggests that explanation answers a contrastive question rather than simply reporting a cause. On that account causal information explains when it identifies what varied, and the reason so many causal claims feel empty is that they name conditions which did not.

subject: 해악 원리와 자유의 한계
title: The harm principle and the limits of liberty
content: A familiar principle in political philosophy holds that the only purpose for which power may rightfully be exercised over a member of a community against his will is to prevent harm to others. The principle is attractive because it draws a line that does not depend on anyone's view of the good life, and it has shaped argument about censorship, drugs, and personal conduct for a century and a half. Its difficulty lies in the word harm. If harm includes any setback to another's interests, then almost every action qualifies, since competition, criticism, and refusal all leave someone worse off, and the principle licenses interference everywhere. If harm is restricted to physical injury, then it permits conduct that ruins lives without touching bodies, and few defenders accept that result. Every attempt to fix the term has therefore imported judgments the principle was meant to avoid. A further problem concerns offence. Conduct that distresses others without damaging their interests occupies an awkward position, and treating distress as harm would return the censorship the principle was designed to block. Most contemporary positions accept that offence may sometimes warrant restriction while insisting that the bar be high, which concedes that the harm principle does not settle cases on its own. It marks where the argument begins rather than where it ends.

subject: 용서와 정의의 긴장
title: Forgiveness and the demands of justice
content: Forgiveness is widely praised as a moral achievement, and yet it sits uneasily with the conviction that wrongdoing deserves a response. If a wrong genuinely merited resentment, then giving up that resentment appears to deny what justice affirmed, and philosophers have asked how the two can both be virtues. The tension is not resolved by calling forgiveness generous, because generosity with what one is owed differs from generosity with what others are owed. One account holds that forgiveness responds to a change in the wrongdoer rather than to the wrong. Where the offender has repudiated what he did, he is no longer the person the resentment was directed at, so releasing it tracks a real alteration instead of ignoring one. This preserves justice while making forgiveness intelligible, and it explains why unrepentant offenders seem harder to forgive. Critics observe that people do forgive without repentance and that we often admire them for it, which the account cannot easily allow. A second position treats forgiveness as the victim's prerogative over her own standing to resent, distinct from any judgment about what the offender deserves. On this view she may release her claim while the wrong remains fully condemned, and third parties retain their own responses. The distinction between personal and impersonal claims does most of the work here.

subject: 세대 간 정의와 자원 배분
title: Justice between generations
content: Decisions about resources reach far beyond the people who make them, since a policy on energy or debt shapes conditions for those not yet born. Political philosophy has therefore asked what the present owes the future, and the question resists the frameworks built for justice among contemporaries because the parties cannot negotiate, cannot reciprocate, and do not yet exist. Contract-based theories struggle first. If justice arises from agreement among those who can benefit one another, then future people have nothing to offer and no place at the table, which delivers a conclusion nobody accepts. Attempts to repair this imagine parties ignorant of which generation they belong to, and that device generates obligations while raising questions about why anyone should reason from a position they know they do not occupy. A second approach avoids agreement entirely, grounding obligation in the interests future people will have whether or not they can press them now. This matches ordinary moral judgment more closely, and its difficulty is one of specification, since the number and identity of future people depend on present choices. What survives every approach is that the burden of proof has shifted. Treating the future as morally weightless is no longer a default that requires no defence, and any policy that discounts it steeply now owes an argument.

subject: 규칙 따르기란 무엇인가
title: What it is to follow a rule
content: Following a rule looks like the simplest thing in the world, and yet philosophers have found that saying what it consists in is remarkably hard. The difficulty appears when we ask what makes a particular continuation of a series correct, since any finite stretch of examples is compatible with infinitely many rules, and nothing in the examples themselves picks one out. A person who has always added two might, on this reasoning, be following a rule that diverges at some point we have not reached. Nor does appealing to what the person intended settle the matter. Whatever mental item accompanied her past applications was also finite, and it stands in need of interpretation exactly as the examples did, so the question simply moves. This regress is what makes the puzzle serious rather than merely clever, because it threatens the idea that meaning determines correctness at all. The most discussed response locates correctness in a practice rather than in any fact about the individual. What makes a continuation right is that it accords with how a community goes on, and the agreement in question is agreement in action rather than in opinion. Critics argue that this substitutes consensus for truth and cannot explain a lone reasoner who is right against everyone. The debate has shaped how philosophers think about meaning, law, and mathematics alike.

subject: 인격과 신체의 관계
title: The person and the body
content: We speak of having a body and of being a person, and the two ways of speaking suggest different relations. If a person merely has a body, then she stands to it as an owner stands to property, and the body could in principle be exchanged. If a person is a body, then damage to it is damage to her, and the ownership language misleads. Moral philosophy cares about the answer because consent, bodily integrity, and what may be done to the dying all rest on it. The ownership picture supports a strong right of control, since an owner may dispose of what is hers, and much of medical ethics has been argued in these terms. Its cost is that it treats the body as external to the person, which sits badly with the experience of illness, where what happens to the body is not something happening to one's property. The identity picture captures that experience and struggles elsewhere, because it makes any alteration of the body an alteration of the person and leaves little room for the ordinary sense that one might have been otherwise embodied. A third position treats the relation as constitutive without being identity, holding that a person is embodied rather than either owning or being a body. This preserves both intuitions, and its defenders concede that the metaphysics remains unsettled.

subject: 예술의 정의와 제도론
title: Defining art through institutions
content: Attempts to define art by a common property have repeatedly failed, since every candidate has been either too narrow to include some accepted works or too broad to exclude ordinary objects. Beauty excludes deliberately ugly works that criticism takes seriously, representation excludes abstraction, and expression admits a great deal that no gallery would show. This record of failure prompted a different strategy, which locates the answer not in the object but in what surrounds it. The institutional account holds that something is a work of art when it has been presented as a candidate for appreciation by someone acting on behalf of the artworld. On this view an ordinary object placed in a gallery becomes art through the act of placing, and no perceptible property need change. The account explains the notorious cases that defeated its rivals, and it explains why the boundary shifts as institutions do. What it gains in coverage it may lose in substance. Critics object that the account is circular, since the artworld is identified by its dealings with art, and that it licenses anything a curator chooses while saying nothing about whether the choice was good. Defenders reply that a definition need not be an evaluation, and that separating the two questions is precisely the advance. The dispute continues because each side wants the definition to do different work.

subject: 장식과 기능, 그리고 정직함이라는 수사
title: Ornament, function, and the rhetoric of honesty
content: Early modern architects argued that decoration was not merely useless but dishonest, since it hid the structure that actually held a building up. Their attack tied ornament to lying and bare walls to honesty, and this pairing proved catchy enough to shape a century of building. Yet the argument rests on a claim worth testing, namely that a building has one truth which its surface either shows or hides. Buildings are not clear in that way. A steel frame is already out of sight beneath its cladding, and the smooth concrete plane that supposedly speaks the truth is itself a finish laid over the bars within. What the reformers offered was therefore not the end of rhetoric but a new rhetoric, one whose words happened to be plainness rather than leaves and scrolls. Those who study craft traditions reach a similar view from another side, since in many places a worked surface carries facts the object could not otherwise state, holding rank, kinship, or debt in patterns that members read at a glance. To call such patterns useless is to take one's own blindness for their emptiness. Ornament on this view is a medium rather than a leftover, and stripping it deletes content instead of clearing anything up. The modern taste for bare form then looks less like a finding about buildings than a claim about which meanings deserve to be seen.

subject: 취향의 사회적 형성
title: How taste is formed
content: Preferences in music, food, and furnishing feel intensely personal, and people defend them as expressions of individual sensibility. Research in cultural sociology complicates this account without quite refuting it, since large surveys find that taste correlates strongly with education and upbringing, and the correlations persist after income is held constant. What people enjoy therefore appears bound up with how they were formed rather than with what they can afford. The mechanism proposed is dispositional rather than deliberate. Children acquire habits of attention from the households in which they grow up, learning which objects reward close inspection and which conversations count as serious, and these habits later present themselves as preferences that seem to arise from nowhere. Because the acquisition is early and largely unremarked, its results feel natural, and their social origin stays invisible precisely to those who hold them. Critics of the framework observe that it explains too much. If every preference expresses a position in a social structure, then it cannot distinguish a judgment reached through sustained attention from one absorbed unreflectively, and it leaves no room for changing one's mind on the merits. Defenders reply that the account describes tendencies rather than destinies. What the dispute leaves standing is that taste is not innocent of history, and that confident reports about one's own preferences are a poor guide to where they came from.

subject: 건축과 신체의 척도
title: Architecture and the measure of the body
content: Buildings are made for bodies, and for most of their history their sizes came from bodies directly, since the units used to set them out were feet, cubits, and paces. This grounding was not merely handy, because many traditions held that shapes drawn from the human figure carried a rightness that random measures lacked, and books across several cultures set out systems tying a column or a door to the frame of a person. Machine production loosened that tie. Materials arrived in fixed sizes set by the factory rather than by the body, so a designer working with them took on a module that no person had settled. Several modern architects answered by building new systems from the measures of an ideal figure, trying to restore the older ground inside a factory process. Those systems were faulted for the figure they picked, since one ideal body cannot stand for the range of people who use a building. What the episode shows is that the appeal to bodily measure was always partly a claim about whose bodies counted. A stair whose steps suit an average adult is hard for a child and unsafe for someone frail, and calling its shape natural hides a decision. Current practice therefore speaks of access rather than of harmony, and that shift turns the question from what looks right to whom a building lets in.
